meta.title: FloodCatch: Physics-Guided Machine Learning for Flood Dynamics Monitoring Between Sentinel-1 Acquisitions
meta.authorsHtml: Jiayi Cai<sup>∗</sup><sup>1</sup>, Marin Heckmann<sup>1</sup>, Julien Elkhiati<sup>1</sup>, Martin Chauvin<sup>1</sup>, Kevin De Vasconcelos<sup>1</sup>, Sofiane Schaack<sup>1</sup>

abstract: Floods are among the most frequent and damaging natural disasters, with impacts across social, economic, and environmental systems. As climate change intensifies extreme rainfall events, both the frequency and severity of floods are increasing. Reliable flood monitoring is therefore essential for early warning and post-event impact assessment. While physics-based hydrological and hydrodynamic models are widely used for flood prediction, they remain constrained by data scarcity, computational complexity, and uncertain initial and boundary conditions. Earth observation, particularly Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR), provides spatially detailed and near all-weather flood mapping; however, satellite revisit intervals are typically too coarse to capture continuous flood dynamics. To address this limitation, FloodCatch proposes a physics-guided machine learning framework for reconstructing flood probability maps at unobserved timestamps. The approach combines unsupervised SAR-based flood segmentation with hybrid spatio-temporal imputation that integrates physical constraints into the learning process. Experiments across multiple flood cycles demonstrate improved temporal continuity and physically coherent flood evolution compared to purely data-driven baselines.

blocks.html: Climate change is intensifying hydrometeorological extremes worldwide, and flooding has become one of the most damaging climate-related hazards. Recent studies indicate that extreme multi-day rainfall events are becoming both more frequent and more intense under a warming climate, directly amplifying flood risk [1]. Reliable flood monitoring is therefore essential for early warning and post-event impact assessment.

Physics-based hydrological and hydrodynamic models remain the operational backbone of flood forecasting. Hydrological components simulate rainfall–runoff processes at the catchment scale, while hydrodynamic models route discharge through river networks and floodplains by solving simplified or full flow equations. However, these models are often constrained by high computational cost, and sensitivity to uncertain initial and boundary conditions [2].

In recent years, Machine Learning (ML) is emerging as an attractive approach to overcome the limitations of physics-based models, by extracting spatiotemporal relationships from historical data, a trend amplified by the growing availability of Earth Observation (EO) products [3, 4]. Among EO sources, Sentinel-1 (S1) Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imagery, operated by ESA under the Copernicus program, is particularly valuable due to its weather independence, especially from cloud cover, and open accessibility [5]. However, the effective revisit frequency of S1, typically ranging from 6 to 12 days, results in relatively low, about 58%, of European flood events capture rate [6], preventing continuous observation of flood dynamics.

Few studies directly address the SAR revisit gap. Dasgupta et al. [7] introduced a CNN-based fusion framework for reconstructing flood maps in the absence of contemporaneous SAR acquisitions. Their feature analysis suggests that static terrain conditions strongly influence the predictions, highlighting the complexity of integrating dynamic hydrological forcing at fine spatial scales.

In parallel, increasing attention has been devoted to physics-guided and hybrid ML approaches that aim to combine data-driven flexibility with physically grounded constraints. The integration of physics and ML can occur bidirectionally: SAR-derived flood products can be assimilated into hydrodynamic models to improve predictions [8, 9], while outputs from physics-based simulations can initialize or constrain ML models in data-sparse conditions or for better generalization [10].

To bridge the SAR revisit gap while preserving physical consistency, we propose FloodCatch, a physics-guided ML framework for reconstructing flood probability maps at unobserved timestamps, i.e., performing temporal imputation by filling in the missing time steps between two consecutive Sentinel-1 acquisitions. This approach relies on the following framework. First, a Split-Based Gaussian Mixture Model (SBGMM) generates consistent flood probability maps across heterogeneous SAR acquisitions. Second, these maps are processed by a hybrid imputation architecture that combines: a spatial encoder–decoder branch for image-based feature extraction from multi-temporal SAR observations, and a physics-constrained temporal branch for modeling flood dynamics under hydrological forcing. The temporal branch integrates runoff sequences through a linear reservoir and redistributes the resulting water volume using a volume-constrained topographic susceptibility model derived from elevation, slope, and proximity to existing water. Finally, a dynamic dual loss with epoch-dependent weighting jointly supervises spatial interpolation and temporal change modeling, enabling physically coherent flood evolution between satellite overpasses.

blocks.html: Model inputs are organized into 6–12 day cycles corresponding to the S1 revisit frequency. Each cycle includes two consecutive S1 acquisitions and intermediate high-resolution SAR imagery from a third-party operator, used as reference to reconstruct flood probability maps at intermediate timestamps.

The first step of the pipeline consists of consistent waterarea segmentation of SAR imagery from heterogeneous sensors and configurations. We adopt an unsupervised split-based strategy [16] that selects representative tiles with low mean backscatter and high standard deviation for model fitting. We extend this strategy by replacing its fuzzy-logic water-likelihood estimator with a GMM, which produces probabilistic estimates for the two classes (land and water). These GMM-derived flood probabilities are then intersected with a permanent water mask from the WorldCover dataset [14] to exclude static water bodies. The proposed method is validated on the KuroSiwo reference dataset [12], which provides expertly annotated flood masks for worldwide S1 flood events.
The SBGMM-derived flood probability maps serve as inputs to the second stage of the pipeline, a physics-guided imputation model illustrated in Figure 1.

The imputation model is first driven by a hydrologically constrained temporal branch that explicitly models flood dynamics under ERA5 runoff forcing. A learnable linear reservoir integrates runoff from th (the beginning of the cycle) to the imputation time th+x (with x hours after th) to estimate an aggregated water volume proxy, following the first-order storage equation:

where U(t) denotes the reservoir storage, qt is the runoff rate, and k is a learnable recession coefficient. Equation (1) is discretely integrated over the interval [th, th+x] to obtain the accumulated water depth Uh+x at the target timestamp.

This volume is then spatially redistributed using a threefactor topographic susceptibility model. Flood propagation is guided by: (i) a low elevation preference, based on the DEM, (ii) a flat terrain preference, based on slope, computed from the DEM; and (iii) proximity to existing water seeds defined by the initial S1 flood map Mh.

The three factors are combined into a normalized weight map controlling water redistribution. Given the resulting weights, a binary search determines the water depth such that the integrated flooded volume matches the reservoirderived volume. This guarantees physical consistency between runoff input and spatial flood extent. The resulting depth map defines a physics-guided temporal prior, which is then transformed into a probabilistic flood mask through an exponential depth-to-probability mapping. An encoder–decoder subsequently refines this prior, allowing the network to learn residual corrections while preserving the physically constrained structure.

In parallel, the spatial branch is implemented as a U- Net–based encoder—decoder architecture with skip connections and FiLM-conditioned decoding, where the normalized duration d ∈[0, 1] modulates feature responses according to the temporal position within the acquisition cycle. This branch processes the flood probability maps Mh, Mh+n and the corresponding SAR images Ih, Ih+n to extract image-based features.

The spatial and temporal predictions are finally fused through a duration-dependent cosine weighting α(d) = 1+cos(2πd), designed to give stronger influence to the physics-guided temporal branch at mid-cycle and greater weight to the spatial branch near the endpoints.
Training employs a dynamic dual Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE) + Soft Dice (SD) [17] loss that supervises the temporal and spatial branches with complementary objectives.

Table 2 compares SBGMM with a global GMM baseline and reports the best and worst mIoU values from supervised models in the original KuroSiwo study for reference. Figure 2 shows a representative example illustrating the performance of the proposed SBGMM.

Regarding imputation, tiles of 256 × 256 pixels at 10 m spatial resolution are used for training, validation, and testing, following a 70/20/10 split. Figure 3 compares the reference flood probability maps with predictions from a purely data-driven spatio-temporal encoder–decoder baseline and the proposed physics-guided model.

SBGMM consistently outperforms the global GMM and achieves competitive performance relative to supervised baselines, despite not relying on labeled training data. It also performs on par with other state-of-the-art unsupervised SAR flood segmentation methods [18].

blocks.html: As shown in Figure 3, the purely data-driven baseline produces quasi-static predictions, with limited spatial redistribution between timestamps. Flooded regions remain concentrated around initial patterns, indicating limited capability to capture physically meaningful flood evolution.

Figure 4 shows the runoff forcing and associated topographic descriptors (DEM and slope) for the same tile. The runoff time series (Figure 4a) exhibits an initial sharp peak followed by secondary pulses and gradual recession.

Consistent with this physically constrained mechanism, the proposed model exhibits clearer structural dynamics than the baseline. Flood expansion follows the runoff evolution while preferentially spreading across low-elevation and low-slope areas, as shown in Figure 4b and Figure 4c. As a result, the spatial distribution aligns more closely with the reference maps, capturing lateral spread rather than simple uniform intensity scaling.

However, some limitations remain. Around the midcycle period, when the temporal branch dominates, predictions appear less spatially sharp compared to the reference. In addition, predicted probabilities tend to be slightly underestimated, suggesting that the current spatial–temporal fusion strategy may attenuate intensity variations and smooth fine-scale boundaries.

blocks.html: This study introduces FloodCatch, a physics-guided SAR flood imputation framework designed to address the Sentinel-1 revisit gap. The model combines spatial image-based feature extraction with a hydrologically constrained temporal branch. Experiments show improved structural evolution and terrain-consistent flood dynamics over purely data-driven baselines. While some limitations remain, particularly in preserving fine-scale flood boundaries at mid-cycle and accurately estimating flood probabilities, the results are promising. Future work will extend the experiments to a broader set of events to enable more comprehensive quantitative assessment and further refine the spatial–temporal fusion strategy.
